newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac tells Clinton NATO command issue "capital".
newsitem.headline: Chirac tells Clinton NATO command issue "capital".

text.p: President Jacques Chirac told U.S. President Bill Clinton that transferring NATO's southern command from an American to a European officer was of "capital importance" to France, according to a leaked letter.

In the October 10 letter, a text of which was obtained by Reuters, Chirac set out France's argument for giving the key post, which controls allied forces in the Mediterranean including Bosnia and the shores of the Middle East and North Africa, to a European.
Diplomatic sources said it was the second personal letter Chirac had written to Clinton on the issue and was sent in reply to the U.S. president's rebuff of his first approach.
Though Washington has flatly rejected France's call, the letter discloses how high France has raised the stakes on the issue.
In a handwritten final note underlining his determination, the French leader said: "The issue of the Southern Command is, in my view, of capital importance."
NATO fellow allies Germany, Italy and Spain have publicly backed the call for Washington to yield the Naples-based AFSOUTH command, which also controls the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

In September, Defence Minister Charles Millon voiced the threat that Paris would freeze its reintegration into NATO's military structure if it did not gain satisfaction on the matter. French officials have not repeated that threat lately.
NATO officials say the dispute is holding up agreement on a fundamental overhaul of the alliance's command structure to adapt to the post-Cold War.
The fact that Chirac has made the issue such a personal test makes it harder for either side to climb down, they say.
"It has become a manhood issue," one official said.

The far-reaching reform, giving a greater role to a European security and defence identity and reducing the number of NATO commands, was due to have been adopted at a foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels this month.
But officials said because of the top-level Franco-American dispute, it was unlikely to be settled until a NATO summit in mid-1997.

In his letter, Chirac praised work under way to give a European deputy to NATO's American Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR) greater responsibily but told Clinton: "I would, nonetheless, like to touch upon a subject of major concern for France and Europe: the Southern Command."

"Political and strategic concerns would assign this Command to a European," he wrote. "For the new transatlantic partnership to take on its full meaning, a balance of responsibilities must be established within the Alliance...

He justified the call by citing "the new importance that we Europeans must place on developments in the Mediterranean Basin, an area so close to us. In demographic, economic, political and strategic terms, the Mediterranean is crucial for Europe.
"For both Europe and the Alliance, it is essential that we Europeans shoulder our responsibilities in the Mediterranean, obviously working closely with the United States," he wrote.

Chirac told Clinton he was "aware of the importance of the operational issues you raise", but added: "It is my conviction ...the appropriate solutions can be found in order to reconcile assigning the Southern Command to a European, preserving the United States' interests in the Mediterranean and maintaining the Alliance's military effectiveness in the region."
He called for "innovative solutions...to address our different concerns".

Diplomats said the French have suggested either putting the Sixth Fleet directly under SACEUR, the top U.S. military commander in Europe, while giving the Naples post to a European, or rotating the Southern Command between an American and a European, with the American to go first.
Both solutions were equally unacceptable to the United States, which was determined to hold on to AFSOUTH, they said.
France's Socialist opposition leader, Lionel Jospin, attacked Chirac on Sunday for taking France back into NATO's military wing, saying Paris had "obtained nothing" in exchange.
"If France could manage during the Cold War being outside NATO's integrated structure, there's no need to go back in now that the Berlin Wall has fallen," Jospin told Europe 1 radio.
"This problem should have been treated first from the European angle. We have obtained nothing. The government and the president have taken the wrong road in this matter," he said.
